title: Understanding N-grams
text: Think about how N-grams work. They capture sequences of N consecutive elements. How might this be problematic when dealing with DNA sequences?

title: Non-consecutive Segments
text: Consider how N-grams might include segments that aren't biologically meaningful. What happens when you have non-consecutive letters being treated as a sequence?

title: Meaningless Segments
text: In DNA, codons are groups of $$3$$ letters. What happens if you capture segments of $$1$$ or $$2$$ letters? Do they have any biological significance?

hintAnswer: Overlapping segments would be included, meaning ATGCA is broken up into $$3$$ overlapping words.
title: Overlapping Segments
text: If you have a DNA sequence like ATGCA, how would N-grams break it down?
choices: Overlapping segments would be included, meaning ATGCA is broken up into $$3$$ overlapping words.
Segments of $$non-consecutive$$ letters would be included, meaning ATGCA could suggest the word AGA.
Segments with $$1$$ or $$2$$ letters have no meaning, which $$N-gram$$ would capture as 'words'.
DNA does not 'wrap around', but $$N-gram$$ would capture $$'wrap-around'$$ segments, like TGG from GGTT.

title: Wrap-around Segments
text: DNA sequences are linear and do not wrap around. How might N-grams mistakenly capture sequences that don't exist in the actual DNA?
